q.t: What is the step pattern of every major scale?
o: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
H W W W H W W
W W W H W W H
q.e: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

q.t: What are the notes of the C major scale?
o: C D E F G A B C
C D E F♯ G A B C
C D E♭ F G A B C
C D E F G A B♭ C
q.e: C major uses only the plain letters — no sharps or flats.

q.t: On the guitar, a whole step (W) is…
q.e: Whole step = 2 half steps = 2 frets.

q.t: How many sharps or flats does C major have?
q.e: None — the half steps land on E–F and B–C.

q.t: Which sharp does G major have?
q.e: G A B C D E F♯ G.

q.t: In sargam, what are the 7 notes?
o: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni
Do Re Mi Fa So La Ti
C D E F G A B
Sa Pa Ma Ga Re Ni Dha
q.e: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni, then Sa again.

q.t: In solfège, step 5 is…
Step 1 of a scale is called the…
q.e: The tonic is home — tunes usually end there.

q.t: How many different notes are in a major scale (before it repeats)?
q.e: 7 notes; the 8th is the first note again, an octave up.

q.t: In sargam, which note matches step 1?
q.e: Sa is home, like do.

q.t: In C major, which steps are the half steps?
q.e: The pattern's half steps (3→4 and 7→8) land on E–F and B–C.

q.t: Why does C major need no sharps or flats?
o: Its half steps land on E–F and B–C
It is the easiest to play
q.e: The pattern's two half steps match the two natural half steps exactly.

q.t: What are the notes of G major?
o: G A B C D E F♯ G
G A B C D E F G
G A B♭ C D E F G
G A B C♯ D E F♯ G
q.e: Follow W W H W W W H from G: the rule forces F♯.

q.t: Why does G major have F♯ and not F?
o: E → F is only a half step; the pattern needs a whole step
F is too low for G major
Every scale must have one sharp
q.e: Step 6 → 7 must be W. E → F is H, so go one further to F♯.

q.t: What is step 7 of C major?
What is step 5 of G major?
What are the notes of D major?
o: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D
D E F G A B C D
D E F♯ G A B C D
D E♭ F G A B♭ C D
q.e: W W H W W W H from D gives F♯ and C♯.

q.t: Why does step 7 (ti / Ni) pull towards home?
o: It is only a half step below home
It is a whole step below home
It is the same note as home
q.e: A half step is a tense, close gap, so the 7th sounds like it wants to move up to the tonic.

q.t: Which interval is step 1 → step 5 of any major scale?
q.e: W W H W = 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7 half steps = perfect 5th.

q.t: Which interval is step 1 → step 3 of any major scale?
q.e: W W = 2 + 2 = 4 half steps = major 3rd.

q.t: What are the notes of A major?
o: A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯ A
A B C D E F G A
A B C♯ D E F G A
A B♭ C D E F G A
q.e: W W H W W W H from A: three sharps — F♯, C♯, G♯.

q.t: What are the notes of F major?
o: F G A B♭ C D E F
F G A B C D E F
F G A A♯ C D E F
F G♯ A B♭ C D E F
q.e: A → B would be a whole step, but the pattern needs a half step there → B♭.

q.t: Why does F major use B♭ and not A♯?
o: Each letter is used once, and A is already there
A♯ is not a real note
q.e: A major scale uses every letter once. With A already used, the next note must be some kind of B.

q.t: How many sharps does E major have?
q.e: E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯ E — F♯, G♯, C♯, D♯.

q.t: How many sharps does D major have?
q.e: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D.

q.t: In the G major scale shape (starting low E fret 3), what is the 3rd note?
You slide the G major shape up 2 frets. Which scale do you get?
q.e: Starting note moves from G to A (2 half steps), and the shape keeps the same step pattern.

q.t: Why can one scale shape be moved to make any major scale?
o: Every major scale has the same step pattern
All scales use the same notes
Frets are all the same width
q.e: Same pattern → same distances → same shape; only the starting fret changes.

q.t: What is step 4 of D major?
In C major, which sargam note is G?
q.e: C D E F G = Sa Re Ga Ma Pa.

q.t: Using W W H W W W H, what is step 7 of E major?
q.e: E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯ — and it can't be E♭ because each letter is used once and E is already there.

q.t: What is step 3 of B♭ major?
q.e: B♭ + W = C, + W = D.

q.t: Which scale is: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭?
q.e: Starts and ends on E♭ and follows W W H W W W H.

q.t: A scale goes C D E F♯ G A B C. Why is it not C major?
o: F♯ makes step 3→4 a whole step
q.e: C major needs a half step at 3→4 (E → F). E → F♯ is a whole step, so the pattern is broken.

q.t: How many half steps from step 1 to step 8 of a major scale?
q.e: W W H W W W H = 2+2+1+2+2+2+1 = 12 — one octave.

q.t: How many half steps from step 1 to step 4?
q.e: W W H = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 — a perfect 4th.

q.t: How many half steps from step 1 to step 6?
q.e: W W H W W = 2+2+1+2+2 = 9 — a major 6th.

q.t: What is the 6th note of A major?
q.e: A B C♯ D E F♯ — step 6 is F♯.

q.t: A tune in G major stops on F♯. Why does it sound unfinished?
o: F♯ is step 7, a half step below home
q.e: Step 7 leans hard towards home (G), so stopping there feels like an unanswered question.

q.t: Which order of scales adds exactly one new sharp each time?
q.e: C (0), G (1: F♯), D (2: + C♯), A (3: + G♯), E (4: + D♯). Each starts a perfect 5th above the last.
